I had prepared for weeks. I rehearsed my speech, even practiced hand gestures. But when the moment came, I froze. Even though I knew my content inside out, I couldn’t speak. People even started whispering. And yet, I smiled, took a deep breath, and tried again. It wasn’t perfect, but even the smallest step forward matters.
What effect does “even though” have in the second paragraph?
What would the tone be like without “even” in the story?
a) She even don’t like music.
b) Even he knows that’s not true.
Replace or add “even” to create emphasis:
a) She came to my birthday. My ex came too, which was surprising.
b) He didn’t call. He didn’t write. He didn’t ___ care.
Make the sentences more natural using “even”:
a) I was tired, but I worked. I was sick, but I worked.
b) Nobody helped me. Not my friends. Not my family.
a) Even he can’t solve it.
b) He can’t solve even it.

Write a short narrative (150+ words) about a surprising experience. Use “even” at least 5 times.
Watch a TED Talk or casual podcast episode. Write down 5 examples of “even” or “even though” and explain the meaning in each context.
Rewrite these using “even” for emphasis or surprise:
I don’t know why she was angry.
He answered the hardest question correctly.
Record yourself telling a story using
at least 4 times. Focus on natural intonation.
Write a dialogue between two coworkers or friends that includes “even”, “even though”, and “even if” at least twice each.
Reflect: Why do you think “even” is hard to translate into Portuguese? Write a paragraph comparing it to “até”, “nem”, or “mesmo”.
